power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Phenomenological characteristics are central to theoretical distinctions among modern memory constructs.
For instance, reexperiencing is often considered diagnostic of episodic recall, with hippocampal reinstatement likely underpinning this characteristic at the neural level.
However, most phenomenology research relies on instruments with content and scoring schemes that embed theoretical assumptions into their measurements.
Here, we explored whether phenomenological characteristics emerge from self-reported memory experiences, as anticipated by episodic memory theory.
We solicited memories from a large online sample, following each response with a novel questionnaire designed to evaluate the phenomenology of individual memories.
We used folded bottom-up factor analyses to examine and validate the global latent factor structure of participants' memory experiences.
Consistent with Tulving's declarative memory framework, our analyses produced five stable dimensions: imagery, autonoetic consciousness, mental time travel, relational memory, and semantic memory.
In order, these dimensions reflect multimodal perceptual reexperiencing, personal meaning, sense of reliving, detailed spatiotemporal context, and conscious use of semantic knowledge during recall.
The semantic memory dimension has no clear predecessor, suggesting the strategic use of general knowledge during recall is a distinct and previously uncharacterized aspect of remembering.
This factor structure generalized across memories elicited by recent and remote episodic prompts.
However, distinct versions of mental time travel and relational memory emerged in response to the semantic prompt, suggesting these dimensions of memory are context-sensitive rather than fixed.

While our findings validate the link between episodic memory and its theorized phenomenological elements, they also invite broader investigation of how phenomenology may vary across different classes of memory.
What does it feel like to remember?

The subjective experience of recall (phenomenology) is central to current definitions of episodic memory, with phenomenology so tightly coupled to these definitions that it is often used as a primary screen for categorizing memories as episodic or nonepisodic (Tulving, 2002).

text.text: While research has offered insight regarding the experience of remembering (for a review, see Chiorri & Vannucci, 2024), instruments assessing characteristics of memory phenomenology (qualia) are commonly developed using top-down methods (e.g., confirmatory factor analysis) to capture theoretical dimensions of episodic memory without testing their underlying premises.

text.text: Here, we tested whether episodic qualia emerge naturally from reports of memory phenomenology, or whether they are synthetic products of theory.
Episodic qualia were initially described in Endel Tulving's Organization of Memory (1972) in which he proposed working definitions of episodic and semantic memory.

text.text: He argued that memory processes information using two specialized systems that interact during recall: episodic memory processes information about personal experiences and temporally locates them in reference to other experiences, and semantic memory organizes information about the meaning and interrelatedness of concepts.

While qualia are commonly considered distinguishing features of episodic memory, Tulving (1985) proposed that the only phenomenological feature that is unique to episodic memory is conscious awareness, or the subjective awareness that a memory is a past personal experience.

text.text: Studies using instruments that assess constructs of episodic memory phenomenology (e.g., imagery, emotional connection, reliving) have provided valuable insights (for a review, see Chiorri & Vannucci, 2024).

text.text: However, we are only aware of three instruments that interrogate the underlying structure of memory phenomenology (Boyacioglu & Akfirat, 2015; Fitzgerald & Broadbridge, 2013; Sutin & Robins, 2007).

text.text: Yet even these studies limited their explorations to hypothesis-driven approaches that constrain the detection of emergent dimensions.

While existing instruments largely organize memory qualia into distinct categories according to episodic theory, memories reported as strongly relived have been correlated with the presence of details, vividness, emotional connection, and continuous imagery (Irish et al., 2008 (Irish et al., , 2011)).

text.text: This finding suggests that characteristics like reliving, details, and emotional connection may be better represented by dimensions that blend qualia across categories, rather than conforming to those discrete categories.

The current study assumes existing instruments reliably measure the dimensions they were designed to measure, questioning only how well they represent the underlying structure of memory phenomenology.
Beyond the analytic method, the narrow range of memory classes used to study memory phenomenology may further limit theoretical development.
Few studies have sampled experiences of memories that cannot be labeled as episodic (for a review, see Chiorri & Vannucci, 2024).

text.text: To further explore this idea, we turned to strength and component-based accounts of memory to establish competing predictions concerning the relationship among qualia.

Drawing on a memory strength account (e.g., Wixted, 2007; Yonelinas, 2002), we imagined that qualia may be rigidly bound, such that the strength of a memory and its qualia rise and fall together (the "iceberg" model).

By contrast, component processes accounts propose that episodic memories recruit separable components that group to meet moment-to-moment retrieval demands (Moscovitch, 1992; Moscovitch et al., 2016).

text.text: In this case, hippocampal, spatial and visual brain areas may contribute spatial orientation and visual imagery qualia.
Yet in memories focused on the sequences of sounds, temporal and auditory qualia may be more prominently observed.
We characterized the dynamic combination of sets of qualia as the "ad hoc" model.
We sampled a variety of memories and their characteristics using a purpose-built instrument that probed experiences associated with individual memories.
We developed prompts to sample three memories with different memory characteristics, including memories that are widely considered episodic and semantic.

Items were adapted from existing instruments and extended with novel content from relevant theoretical concepts, enabling our instrument to assess the breadth of Tulving's (2002) declarative memory framework.

text.text: We then ran a family of exploratory factor analyses (EFA) to test and validate the emergent structure of declarative memory phenomenology from the natural variation of participants' reports.

This cross-validation approach was designed to investigate whether the emergent structure of declarative memory phenomenology better aligns with theoretical models than other possible constructs, and whether traditionally recognized qualia are recovered from participants' reports of phenomenology when experiences are free to organize according to their natural covariance structure.
Using our novel instrument, participants evoked three different classes of memory and rated the phenomenology of each reported memory.

We then tested our research question using a two-part analytic strategy: whether there is a global latent factor structure of phenomenology, and whether this structure depends on how memories are evoked.

To test for a global factor structure that is stable across prompts, we divided the data into three mixed-prompt folds and conducted EFAs to identify and validate the global structure of phenomenology.
We expected to identify and replicate a factor structure that broadly aligns with Tulving's theoretical framework.

Since these analyses mixed classes of memories that are expected to produce different memory characteristics, this finding would suggest that phenomenological structure is a stable global feature of memory.
Finally, we surveyed our results for possible evidence of a strength-or component-inspired qualia structure.
If the structure has promptdependent (component-inspired) rather than global (strength-inspired) structural properties, this would be revealed by prompt-specific EFAs.
To test whether prompt-dependent structure exists, we ran three prompt-specific EFAs.

Given the theoretical distinction between episodic and semantic memories, we did not expect the global structure to fully generalize to each of the prompt-specific analyses and we expected factors to look different in retrievals that were episodic versus semantic.

text.text: Computer-Guided Recall.
We adapted the Autobiographical Interview (Levine et al., 2002) instructions to an online Qualtrics survey that prompted the recall of three different autobiographical memories.
text.formatted: We adapted the Autobiographical Interview <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Levine et al., 2002)</ref> instructions to an online Qualtrics survey that prompted the recall of three different autobiographical memories.

text.text: The survey started with a screen showing the general instructions, before proceeding to the specific recall prompts.
Each prompt included the target life period for the memory and a short description of the type of information expected, including examples (See Supplementary Materials S1 for the complete script).
For the two prompts that targeted specific experiences, participants were shown the standard instructions with embedded follow-up probes.
For the prompt that targeted general experiences, instructions and probes were adapted to encourage participants to think about their overall experiences.

Specifically, we prompted retrieval of a recent event (a specific experience from last week), a remote event (a specific experience from childhood), and a period summary (general experiences from childhood).

The first prompt called for content widely regarded as episodic, since it has had little time for consolidation while the second called for content that may remain episodic, albeit possibly supplemented by semantic scripts.

In contrast, the last prompt called for content widely regarded as semantic since general autobiographical knowledge lacks spatiotemporal specificity (Conway & Pleydell Pearce, 2000; Levine et al., 2002).
text.formatted: In contrast, the last prompt called for content widely regarded as semantic since general autobiographical knowledge lacks spatiotemporal specificity <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Conway & Pleydell Pearce, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Levine et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: We developed a 53-item self-report questionnaire that was administered following each computer-guided recall prompt to quantify the expression of declarative memory phenomenology.

We adapted existing items assessing episodic memory phenomenology (see Supplementary Materials S2 for schedule of influences) and created novel items assessing conscious use of general knowledge, concepts, and ideas.

This questionnaire included items identifying traditional elements of episodic memory content (e.g., spatiotemporal specificity, mental imagery, conscious awareness), semantic memory content (e.g., conceptual information), and features associated with memory quality (e.g., elements of memory construction).
See Supplementary Items S3 for the complete list.
All items were refined into simple and concise sentences, using similar sentence structure to assist comprehension and speed of completion.
Wherever reasonable, items were phrased to focus on the experience of a specific recall.
All items used a 5-point scale (generally,1 = strongly disagree to5 = strongly agree, although 18 items used custom anchors; see Supplementary Materials S3 for details).

Item order was randomized within four blocks that were themselves triaged to prioritize sampling information that was expected to fade the fastest, ensuring that the most time-sensitive content was captured before the integrity of the memory degraded.

Items in the first two blocks probed the experience of recall (e.g., sense of immersion and mental imagery), items in the third block largely probed memory construction (e.g., ease of recall and use of conceptual information), and items in the fourth block probed fixed features of the memory (e.g., when and where it occurred).
Participants completed the study online using a survey hosted on Qualtrics.
Following collection of informed consent, they completed a demographic questionnaire and proceeded to the computerguided recall portion of the IAE.
Participants were given a prompt corresponding to one of three conditions.
After spending 1 min writing a brief description, they completed the IAE questionnaire about their memory.
This sequence was repeated until all three randomly ordered prompts were complete.
The expected time to complete the study was approximately 25 min.
Upon completion, participants were automatically thanked and debriefed.
To address ceiling and floor effects, IAE items with an extreme value as the median were removed from further analysis (I14, I15, I26, I41, I42).

Seven additional items were omitted because they assessed attention (I30), were focused on the written narrative (I16, I17), were subject to demand characteristics (I40), had categorical responses that varied on multiple dimensions (I1), or created an artifactual dimension (opposing vantage points) that pulled on phenomenologically relevant items and obscured the construct of interest (I4, I5).
The final factor analysis included 41 IAE items.

Any memory with a description that was insufficient to determine compliance (<15 characters or unrelated to prompt; n = 4), with a failed attention check (n = 16), or with a missing response (n = 84) was omitted from analysis.

Capturing 12% of the variance and consisting of eight items, we named the fourth factor relational memory.

text.text: Since the global structure of memory phenomenology held across two of the three prompt specific analyses, this pattern is more consistent with a prompt-specific effect than with sampling variability.
This suggests that the structure of phenomenology may be context-dependent rather than universal, an idea that will be further explored in section 4.3.
Here, we investigated the emergent structure of memory phenomenology.

Using an empirical approach that mixed classes of memories expected to produce different memory characteristics, we distinguished and replicated five qualia of declarative memory across three folds of our data: imagery, autonoetic consciousness, MTT, relational memory, and semantic memory.
While these factors emerged naturally from participants' reports of memory phenomenology, they showed varying degrees of alignment with established instruments.
Notably, the semantic memory factor has no clear predecessor in the literature.
We then explored whether this factor structure depends on how memories are evoked by testing the stability of this structure in each prompt from which it was derived.

As expected, we found that the structure fully generalized to both event prompts but not the period summary, which suggests memory phenomenology has prompt-dependent rather than global structural properties.
These findings support and extend Tulving's (2002) framework, and they are more consistent with a component-inspired "ad hoc" structure than a strength-inspired "iceberg" qualia structure.

text.text: We found evidence that coherent factors emerge naturally from participants' reports, such that there was a cluster of four moderately to strongly intercorrelated episodic memory dimensions.

This cluster of episodic dimensions included two factors representing facets of conscious awareness (autonoetic consciousness and MTT), the only quale that Tulving (1985) identified as uniquely episodic.

text.text: Consistent with this practice, the relational memory factor may represent a distinct and necessary dimension of episodic phenomenology that distinguishes between specific experiences and general knowledge of events.
Broadly construed, the structure we observed provides bottom-up support for core premises of episodic memory theory.
When compared to studies using hypothesis-driven approaches, our exploratory methodology revealed alternative characterizations of memory constructs.
Aspects of memory detail and vividness tend to be investigated as a single dimension (Boyacioglu & Akfirat, 2015; Sutin & Robins, 2007).

text.text: Our analysis, however, placed these in the larger construct of relational memory, which includes spatiotemporal and chronological features of recall.

Although it may seem more logical for elements like detail and vividness to be independent or combine with mental imagery, we found evidence that they are closely related to spatiotemporal and relational elements of memory.
That is, memories that are highly detailed and vivid tend to be high in spatiotemporal features, but not necessarily in imagery.

Consistent with scene construction theory and research showing the importance of spatial context in memory representations (e.g., Hassabis & Maguire, 2007; Robin et al., 2018), this finding suggests the importance of spatiotemporal features in the reconstruction of memories.

While the strong correlation between relational memory and imagery factors suggests perceptual content often accompanies relational memory, their separability indicates that richly detailed memories are anchored in spatiotemporal structure rather than perceptual imagery.
The cross-loading of thoughts and emotions on autonoetic consciousness and imagery is yet another pattern that was only revealed through the use of bottom-up analysis.
Metacognitions like thoughts and emotions reflect a person's state of mind and affect at a given moment in time, constituting both self-referential and perceptual experiences.
Therefore, these elements should be expected to bridge dimensions of autonoetic consciousness and imagery.
This notion is consistent with research showing that emotional connection during recall is correlated with experiences of imagery and reliving (Irish et al., 2008 (Irish et al., , 2011)).

text.text: Our last factor, semantic memory, has no clear predecessor in the literature on memory phenomenology.
To the best of our knowledge, no questionnaires exist that probe for a potential phenomenological profile of semantic recall (for a review, see Chiorri & Vannucci, 2024).

text.text: The closest analog we found is the Survey of Autobiographical Memory (Palombo et al., 2013).

text.text: This tool, however, only measures perceived general ability to recall facts rather than the use of general knowledge during recall.

The semantic memory factor, by contrast, assesses the conscious experience of using semantic knowledge during individual recollections, and it does not include any characteristics that are traditionally considered episodic.

This factor can be interpreted as having two thematic subgroups: one describing the use of general knowledge to construct or supplement individual memories, and a second evaluating difficulty remembering and the absence of personal connection.
These groups measure the use of active strategic processes and the absence of episodic memory during recall, respectively.
Considered on its own, the second subgroup could be interpreted as reflecting memory failure.
This subgroup-based interpretation, however, evaluates the semantic memory factor in isolation, ignoring its relationship with other factors.
If the semantic memory factor actually represented memory failure, then we would expect to see a strong negative relationship between it and the other four factors.
Instead, weak interfactor correlations with semantic memory were observed, suggesting it is largely independent.

Since the semantic memory factor was robustly detected in all three classes of autobiographical memory recall, and it shared limited variance with the other factors, it may represent a distinct mode of retrieval that supports the recall of different classes of declarative memory.
In effect, when we have an absence of episodic memory during recall (e.g., fewer details), we may increase our reliance on active strategic processes to fill in the blanks and smooth out our memory.
This notion is consistent with theoretical accounts of semantic memory (Irish & Piguet, 2013; Tulving, 2002).

text.text: We found evidence that the global structure of declarative memory phenomenology was stable across memories elicited by event prompts but not period summary prompts.
Imagery, autonoetic consciousness, and semantic memory factors were consistently found to have similar items loading onto them.
However, when period summaries were prompted, the MTT and relational memory factors were distinctive.
For the global structure, MTT was associated with general recreations of the original experience, but for period summary prompts, vivid dynamic imagery also loaded onto the factor.

For the global structure, relational memory included items that contextualized spatiotemporal and metacognitive features of memory, but these were not associated in the period summary case, leaving the factor only with items associated with temporal sequencing.

Despite these differences, the period summary prompt was still associated with five differently organized EFA factors that were each interpretable and internally consistent, and its overall model fit approximated that of the global structure.
We interpreted this as an illustration of how the relevant phenomenological dimensions of recall may shift as a function of the type of memory under interrogation.

This differentiation is not consistent with sampling variability: the core global structure was stable across both event prompts, while the period summary prompt showed distinct organization in only two factors.
The period summary instructions were designed to elicit personal memories that were not grounded in a specific time and place.
These memories should be semantic in nature according to traditional definitions, which implies they should only produce an awareness of acquired knowledge (Tulving, 1985).
text.formatted: These memories should be semantic in nature according to traditional definitions, which implies they should only produce an awareness of acquired knowledge <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Tulving, 1985)</ref>.

text.text: By this account, it would not be surprising to detect the semantic memory factor.

The alignment of imagery with MTT in this prompt, though unexpected, can be similarly explained by Tulving's (2002) supposition that imagery is a correlate of memory quality rather than a defining feature of episodic memory.
text.formatted: The alignment of imagery with MTT in this prompt, though unexpected, can be similarly explained by <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Tulving's (2002)</ref> supposition that imagery is a correlate of memory quality rather than a defining feature of episodic memory.

text.text: Since Tulving (1985) considered conscious awareness to be the defining feature of episodic memory, the continued detection of factors assessing autonoetic consciousness and MTT in a prompt type that does not meet the definitional criteria for episodic memory is puzzling.
text.formatted: Since <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Tulving (1985)</ref> considered conscious awareness to be the defining feature of episodic memory, the continued detection of factors assessing autonoetic consciousness and MTT in a prompt type that does not meet the definitional criteria for episodic memory is puzzling.

text.text: An explanation for this counterintuitive result can be found in Conway and Pleydell-Pearce's (2000) model of autobiographical memory.

text.text: Suggesting that autobiographical memory has a hierarchical organization, this model implies that semantic information about the self retains access to the source information from which it was derived.

If this produces contextual tags that connect personal semantic information to its original episodic traces, then recalling period summaries might coactivate networks of episodic content and associated qualia.
This is consistent with neural evidence showing recruitment of episodic memory systems during semantic retrieval tasks (Sheldon & Moscovitch, 2012).
text.formatted: This is consistent with neural evidence showing recruitment of episodic memory systems during semantic retrieval tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Sheldon & Moscovitch, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: While our blind rating procedure provided evidence of general compliance with the prompt-level instructions, a review of participant responses revealed several memory descriptions that blended episodic content into period summaries.

Regardless of the mechanism, the detection of autonoetic consciousness and MTT in a prompt that is expected to produce semantic recollections calls into question Tulving's proposition that autonoetic consciousness and MTT are defining features of episodic memory.
Our strength-inspired "iceberg" model predicts covariance of qualia, whereas the componentinspired "ad hoc" model predicts separaration.

Consistent with the former prediction, each of our hierarchical omega analyses showed support for a common general factor, and we observed moderately strong interfactor correlations among four of the five identified factors (with the fifth factor showing weak correlation with the others).
However, we did still observe a partially separable multidimensional structure, and at least 70% of the variance was unique to each factor.
The iceberg model also predicts stability in qualia structure across memory classes (event prompts versus period summary prompt) whereas the "ad hoc" account anticipates variation.
A five-factor structure was detected across analyses, but MTT and relational memory factors reorganized when prompts were non-episodic.
Accordingly, while the qualia analysis offers some positive support for both models, the iceberg model is not easily reconciled with the observed variation in structure across classes of memory.

To further explore the relationship between observed factors and component process accounts (Hassabis & Maguire, 2007; Moscovitch et al., 2016), we compared our results with the network of component processes identified by Hassabis and Maguire (2007; see Box 2).
text.formatted: To further explore the relationship between observed factors and component process accounts <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Hassabis & Maguire, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Moscovitch et al., 2016)</ref>, we compared our results with the network of component processes identified by Hassabis and Maguire (2007; see Box 2).

text.text: Five of the nine identified processes map loosely onto factors in the current study: the visual imagery process resembles a facet of the imagery factor; the processes of autonoetic consciousness and self are both related to the autonoetic consciousness factor; the subjective time process resembles the MTT factor; and the narrative process is related to facets of the relational memory factor.

The remaining four processes have no clear counterparts in the current study, including scene construction, which was most closely represented by two spatial-context proxies (spatial immersion and clarity) that aligned with different factors in the event prompt (MTT and relational memory, respectively).

The spatial context items were assigned to the same factor in the period summary prompt, wherein a group of richness items (spatial clarity, vividness, details) diverged from items detailing temporal relationships between event elements, and aligned with the sensation of spatial immersion while reliving a memory.

The joint-factor relationship between ratings of richness and reliving in memory retrievals that span extended periods of time may be indicative of increased abstraction of memory content across multiple experiences, leading people to integrate experiences across the period as a whole such that values of richness and reliving covary.

Since event and period summary prompts elicit different task demands (describe single event versus synthesize extended time), changes in qualia structure in the period summary prompt are broadly consistent with the theory that memory recruits different component processes to meet task demands (Hassabis & Maguire, 2007; Moscovitch et al., 2016).

text.text: The current results may in this way be compatible with a broadly networked, hippocampally based retrieval process that recruits distinct regions associated with individual qualia-based components as needed (Hassabis & Maguire, 2007; Moscovitch et al., 2016; Poppenk et al., 2013), wherein factor scores may offer valuable insights into individual versus scaled recruitment of qualia-based components and their related brain regions.

text.text: As with all survey-based research, the emergent factor structure observed in the current study may reflect covariance driven by surface features (e.g., item wording), rather than by memory content.

However, the majority of the IAE items were adapted from validated instruments and we reviewed response patterns to determine the suitability of each item for analysis, removing any that might destabilize the factor structure.

We then replicated this structure across three independent subsamples, providing further evidence that the observed structure represented stable covariance in the data instead of sample-or item-specific artifacts.
Next, the IAE does not include an item that assesses recall success.
We were, however, able to review memory descriptions to confirm general compliance.
Still, an item assessing recall success would be helpful for distinguishing between semantic recall and memory failure.
Finally, our analyses were constrained by the assumptions of EFA, which requires all responses to be independent.
While we were able to investigate natural variance in responses across subsamples of mixed or isolated prompt types, our analyses only ever contain one response per participant.
As a result, we were unable to account for any variance attributable to individual differences.
That said, an exploratory analysis that included all available responses per participant (up to three, across all conditions) again showed the same factor structure.
The reintroduction of non-independence suggests that individual differences did not substantially distort the observed covariance among items.
Still, future work should attempt to disentangle these contributions.
There is growing evidence that declarative memory cannot be cleanly divided into categories that are purely episodic and semantic (Bontkes et al., 2025; Renoult et al., 2012; Tanguay et al., 2023).

text.text: To date, there has been little research on the phenomenology of memories that do not meet strict episodic criteria, let alone qualia indicative of the use of semantic memory during recall (for a review, see Chiorri & Vannucci, 2024).

text.text: In the current study, we examined recollections that were expected to be more semantic than episodic, but this is only an introductory investigation.

Real-world memory use commonly requires summarizing or synthesizing information across memories until they no longer adhere to the strict spatiotemporal boundaries of episodic memory (e.g., high-level summaries of single experiences and descriptions of repeated events; Conway & Pleydell-Pearce, 2000; D'Argembeau, 2020), meaning there are other types of declarative memory that may not adhere to the global structure we identified in this study.

text.text: Moving forward, it will be important to examine whether there are other classes of memory that produce distinct phenomenological profiles.
Moving beyond hypothesis-driven approaches to memory phenomenology, we showed that qualia are discoverable using bottom-up analyses of subjective experiences across probed classes of memory.

Consistent with Tulving's (2002) framework and validating the link between episodic memory and its theorized phenomenological dimensions, the observed five-factor structure included traditional dimensions of episodic memory and a novel factor querying the strategic use of semantic memory during recall.

text.text: While all five dimensions were consistently detected in mixed and specific subgroup analyses, our analysis of the period summary prompt produced distinct versions of MTT and relational memory factors.
That is, MTT absorbed items related to vivid re-experiencing while relational memory lost items that contextualized the memory.

This divergence was not consistent with sampling variability, hinting that memory phenomenology is prompt dependent such that it shifts in response to the class of memory being recalled as predicted by a component-inspired "ad hoc" account of qualia structure.
This finding encourages further investigation of prompt-dependent effects, as well as caution when applying traditional one-size-fits-all methods to the study of memory phenomenology.

Our interest is not so much in what you choose to discuss, but rather how you describe your experience.
